title: Private Deployments - VPC & On-Prem Comprehensive Deployment and Day-2 Guide
author: Asha Patel
summary: Comprehensive guide for Redwood Private deployments (VPC and on-prem): reference architectures, on-prem packaging, networking & security prerequisites, day-2 operational playbooks, upgrade and rollback procedures, and a customer requirements library.
body:
Purpose:
This document is the canonical reference for engineering, customer success, and solutions teams running Redwood Private (VPC and on-prem) deployments. It consolidates architecture options, operational runbooks, packaging details, and the set of customer requirements we ask for during pre-sales and onboarding. Use this doc during scoping, presales security reviews, installation, and ongoing operations.

Audience:
- Platform engineers and SREs responsible for operating Redwood Private
- Solutions engineers and CSMs validating customer environments
- Customers running private control plane or on-prem data plane deployments

Contents (high level):
1) Goals and constraints
2) Reference architectures (VPC, hybrid, fully on-prem)
3) Networking & security prerequisites (VPC peering, KMS, IAM, firewall rules)
4) On-prem packaging and installer options (k8s operator, air-gapped tarball)
5) Day-2 operations (monitoring, backups, scaling, patch windows)
6) Upgrade & rollback procedures (canary rollouts, db migrations, rollback steps)
7) Customer requirements library (checklist for pre-sales)
8) Ownership, runbooks, links and appendix

1. Goals and constraints- Support two primary private deployment modes: VPC (customer-managed cloud/VPC) and on-prem (customer datacenter / air-gapped).- Provide repeatable, auditable installation and day-2 operations procedures with measurable SLOs.- Minimize drift between Hosted/Dedicated and Private experiences (APIs, routing, observability).- Offer safe upgrade/rollback paths with database change governance and routine canary deployments.

2. Reference architectures
Overview: We support three common patterns. The diagrams below are described textually; links to detailed diagrams are in Related Pages.

2.1. VPC (customer-managed cloud) - recommended for most enterprise customers
Components:
- Control plane: Redwood-managed (optional for fully private customers). If customer chooses Private control plane, the control plane runs in customer VPC as a set of management services (rwd-controlplane).
- Data plane: rwd-inference-runtime and rwd-packager running in customer VPC (EKS/GKE/AKS) or on-prem K8s.
- Networking: Private subnets for worker nodes, management subnet for admin services, NAT gateway for outbound only where required, optional public ALB/NLB for customer-exposed endpoints behind customer WAF.
- Integrations: Customer KMS (CMK), S3-compatible blob store for model artifacts, internal Docker registry, and VPC endpoints for storage and secrets.

2.2. Hybrid (control plane managed by Redwood; data plane in customer VPC)
- Use when customers require minimal operational overhead but strict data residency. Control plane remains in Redwood cloud with mutual TLS and mTLS-based service links to customer data plane.

2.3. Fully on-prem / air-gapped
- All components run within customer network. Packaging delivered as a tarball (airgap bundle) with installer and operator image tarballs and OCI registry bundle. Requires an internal registry, an internal key management service (HSM/KMS), and a stitcher for metrics to be consumed by the customer Prometheus/Grafana stack.

3. Networking & security prerequisites (checklist)
Provide this checklist to customers during scoping. All required items must be completed prior to install window.

Minimum networking table (example):
| Requirement | Example value | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| CIDR ranges | 10.0.0.0/16 | VPC must provide subnets for control and data plane
| Private subnets | 3 across availability zones | Worker nodes & stateful services
| NAT / egress | NAT Gateway or egress proxy | For updates, license activation (if required)
| Load balancer | NLB for gRPC, ALB for HTTP | TLS termination can be on customer LB or on pods
| DNS | Private Route53 or internal DNS | Required for service discovery

Firewall and ports (minimum):
- 6443 (Kubernetes API) - admin access only from jump hosts / management CIDRs
- 2379-2380 (etcd, if using self-hosted cluster) - restricted to control plane nodes
- 9000 / 9001 (rwd-inference runtime gRPC & metrics) - restricted to customer appwoorkloads and Redwood control plane where applicable
- 9090 (Prometheus), 3100 (Loki push) - restricted to monitoring network

Identity & encryption requirements: 
- KMS: Customer CMK in AWS KMS or HSM for on-prem. We require envelope encryption for model artifacts.
- IAM: Minimum roles (node profile, artifact-reader, kms-decrypt) and a service account for the Redwood operator with least privilege.
- mTLS: Operator communicates with Redwood SaaS control plane using mTLS mutual auth when hybrid - customer provides CA chain.

4. On-prem packaging & installer options
We maintain two packaging flows: cloud-native operator (recommended) and air-gapped installer (for restricted environments).

4.1 Operator-based install (recommended for k8s environments)
- Supported k8s: 1.24 - 1.28 (EKS/GKE/AKS and self-hosted).
- Kubernetes resources: rwd-operator (Deployment), rwd-runtime (StatefulSet), rwd-sidecar (DaemonSet for node-local cache), rwd-config (ConfigMap/Secret), rwd-pvc (StorageClass recommended: gp3/fast-ssd or Ceph/Mina).

Quick install (example commands):
1) Add repo and CRD:
   kubectl apply -f https://packages.redwood.ai/private/releases/2026.07/crds.yaml
2) Install operator:
   helm repo add redwood https://packages.redwood.ai/private/charts
   helm install rwd-operator redwood/rwd-operator --namespace redwood --create-namespace \
     --set image.tag=2026.07 --set rbac.create=true
3) Create runtime CR:
   cat > runtime.yaml <<EOF
   apiVersion: rwd.redwood.ai/v1
   kind: InferenceRuntime
   metadata:
     name: rwd-runtime-prod
     namespace: redwood
   spec:
     replicas: 4
     gpu: a10g
     storageClassName: fast-ssd
     modelStore: s3://customer-model-bucket/path
   EOF
   kubectl apply -f runtime.yaml

Notes: Set replicas based on throughput targets in sizing table below. The operator will create StatefulSets and PVCs, install sidecars, and configure liveness/readiness probes.

4.2 Air-gapped / on-prem tarball install
- Use for customers without internet egress. Packaging includes:
  - OCI image tarballs for operator and runtime
  - Helm charts packaged offline
  - Pre-seeded CRDs and manifest templates
  - SHA256 checksums and signed manifest (PGP)

Air-gap install steps (summary):
1) Import images to local registry: docker load + docker push to internal registry
2) Apply CRDs and install operator from local Helm repo
3) Configure secrets for local KMS/HSM and internal blob store
4) Run a validation script (rwd-validate-install) that checks port reachability, DNS, and KMS access

4.3 Packaging specifics and versioning
- Semantic versioning: major.minor.patch (e.g., 2026.07.1).
- Signed artifacts: every release has an associated SHA256 and PGP signature. Verify signatures during air-gapped installs.

5. Day-2 operations
This section lists operational tasks, observed SLOs, monitoring coverage, and routine maintenance.

5.1 SLOs & thresholds (example)
- Token generation latency (p50/p95): target p50 <= 30ms, p95 <= 150ms for small models (up to 2k context) when provisioned with <X batch latency policy>.
- Availability: 99.9% per route (computed monthly), error rate <0.5% (5xx and timeout).
- Model load time: 60s median for warm cache; cold start time depends on local disk speed and quantization.

5.2 Monitoring & alerts (recommended stacks)
- Metrics: Prometheus exporter (rwd-metrics), per-route latency histograms, per-node GPU utilization (nvidia-dcgm exporter), disk IO, and PVC usage.
- Logs: Fluentd/Loki collector for application logs and operator logs.
- Traces: Jaeger/OpenTelemetry for request flows (optional for air-gapped).

Suggested alert thresholds (examples):
- Alert: inference.latency_p95 > 300ms for 5m -> Sev2, notify #private-ops and SRE oncall
- Alert: node.gpu.utilization > 95% for 10m -> Sev2, suggest scale up or batch policy change
- Alert: model-load.failures > 3 per 15m -> Sev1 if impacts >10% requests

5.3 Routine operations
- Weekly:
  - Check available disk and PVC capacity; prune old model artifacts (>90 days)
  - Validate backup job status (etcd/DB snapshots)
- Monthly:
  - Rotate service account keys and audit KMS access logs
  - Run canary inference against golden prompt set and compare outputs to baseline (quality regression check)
- Quarterly:
  - Security patching window for K8s nodes and container runtime (coordinate with customer windows)

5.4 Scaling guidance
- Horizontal scaling: increase replicas in runtime CR based on p95 latencies and GPU utilization.
- Vertical scaling: switch to larger GPU (a100 -> a10g) if throughput per GPU is limiting.

6. Upgrade & rollback procedures
We enforce controlled upgrades with canaries and staged rollouts. All DB migrations are backward compatible or guarded by feature flags.

6.1 Pre-upgrade checklist
- Run rwd-health-check and ensure all alerts are green
- Backup control/data plane databases (etcd/pg) and S3 model store snapshot
- Ensure operator images are fetched and checksums verified
- Notify stakeholders and open maintenance window (include oncall escalation plan)

6.2 Rolling upgrade (operator and runtime) - recommended flow
1) Create a release tag and push images to registry
2) Deploy operator update to management namespace and verify operator health
3) Start a 5% canary: patch runtime CR to add canaryRevision: "2026.07" for a subset (label selector) of pods
4) Run golden prompt test suite against canary instances (pass rate >= 99% for deterministic prompts)
5) If pass, gradually increase traffic to 25% -> 50% -> 100% over a scheduled window.
6) Monitor latency/error rates and model outputs during ramp.

6.3 Rollback procedure (if canary fails)
- Immediate actions:
  1) Route traffic away from canary pods (kubectl patch Service to remove label selector)
  2) Scale down failing revision pods: kubectl scale sts rwd-runtime-2026-07 --replicas=0
  3) Scale back previous stable revision to previous replica count
  4) Revert CR image tag to stable and redeploy operator if necessary
- Postmortem: capture failing logs, model diffs, and open a JIRA for root cause analysis with priority P0/P1 as needed.

6.4 DB migration guidance
- Prefer online, nonblocking migrations. If a migration requires a breaking schema change, perform it in two phases: write-compatible then read-compatible. Always include a tested rollback migration script and validate with a restore/restore-verify step.

7. Customer requirements library (pre-sales checklist)
Provide this checklist to Solutions and CSMs to collect during scoping. Use the answers to generate a deployment plan and SOW.

Network & Infrastructure:
- Cloud provider and region(s)
- VPC CIDR, subnet counts, AZ distribution
- NAT/egress policy and proxy details
- Internal registry (URI), registry credentials format
- Blob store (S3/Azure Blob/MinIO) with example bucket and prefix

Identity & Secrets:
- KMS type and key ARN (AWS KMS, Hashicorp Vault, HSM)
- Service account model and required IAM roles
- Does customer require BYOK (bring-your-own-key)?

Security & Compliance:
- SOC2 / ISO / FedRAMP requirements and required controls
- Data residency rules (where logs and tokens may be stored)
- Audit log retention period (e.g., 1 year)

Operational constraints:
- Maintenance windows and blackout periods
- Oncall rotation and escalation contacts
- Backup retention policy and RTO/RPO targets

8. Runbooks and common playbooks (operational recipes)
Examples (abbreviated):

8.1 Runbook: High inference error rate (500s)
Steps:
1) Identify impacted routes: prometheus query: sum(rate(http_request_errors_total{job="rwd"}[5m])) by (route)
2) Check model pod logs (kubectl logs -l app=rwd-runtime -n redwood --since=15m)
3) Check disk pressure (kubectl top nodes) and OOM events (kubectl describe pod)
4) If caused by model corruption or missing artifacts, trigger model reload: kubectl annotate inferencejob/<id> rwd.io/reload=true
5) If degraded across nodes, scale up replicas or divert traffic to fallback model variant

8.2 Runbook: Failed upgrade canary
Steps:
1) Pause rollout (kubectl patch rollout)
2) Route traffic away from canary and revert to stable revision (see Upgrade & rollback section)
3) Collect logs and attach to incident in PagerDuty

Appendix A - Sizing reference (example)
| Workload class | GPU type | min nodes | recommended PVC | notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Small dev / proof | none (cpu) | 2 | 50 GB | For API testing and low throughput
| Medium production | a10g | 3 | 500 GB | Multi-AZ recommended, use batching settings
| High throughput | a100 80GB | 4 | 2 TB | Use model sharding and optimized kernels

Appendix B - Verification checklist (post-install)
- Operator health: kubectl get deploy -n redwood rwd-operator -> availableReplicas == desired
- Runtime pods healthy: kubectl get sts -n redwood rwd-runtime -> readyReplicas == desiredReplicas
- Metrics ingestion: check Prometheus job "rwd-metrics" for last scrape
- Golden prompt smoke tests: pass rate >= 99% for deterministic tests

Appendix C - Example alert rule (Prometheus)
- name: RWDLatencyHigh
  expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(rwd_inference_latency_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route)) > 0.3
  for: 5m
  labels: severity=page
  annotations: summary="rwd p95 latency > 300ms"

Contact & escalation
If a customer incident is detected, open PagerDuty Redwood-Private-Ops and follow the oncall rotation. For legal/compliance questions, route to security-and-compliance@redwood.ai.

Document maintenance
This guide is maintained by eng-private-deployments. Major updates should be coordinated with Product and Security. For edits: update the release tag in the header and add a short changelog entry at the top of the document.
